compiled_state.title: /dso:fix-bug: classifying visual change as not behavioral -> skips RED test authoring
compiled_state.author: Test
compiled_state.description:
### 1. Technical Environment

* **code_version:** e2077dec166e955eadc43cc62edbf46d2ec22001
* **Context Scope:** Test project — /dso:fix-bug invoked on a ticket describing a visual/CSS/layout change

### 2. Incident Overview

* **Scenario Type:** User-Flagged Behavior

#### Expected Behavior

Per the behavioral testing standard (`plugins/dso/skills/shared/prompts/behavioral-testing-standard.md`) and `/dso:fix-bug` TDD contract, the skill must write at least one RED test for every behavioral change before implementing the fix. Visual changes (CSS classes, layout, rendered output, component appearance) are behavioral — they affect observable system output. The skill should author a RED test that captures the visual change before writing the fix.

#### Actual Behavior

When the change under investigation is primarily visual (e.g., CSS styling, layout adjustments, component rendering), `/dso:fix-bug` classifies the change as "not behavioral" and skips the RED test authoring step entirely. No test is written. The fix proceeds without a failing test that would validate the visual change.

### 5. Skills and Workflows

* **Active Workflow:** `/dso:fix-bug` TDD cycle (RED → GREEN → UPDATE)
* **Skills Invoked:** `/dso:fix-bug`

comments.body:
### Agent Reasoning (captured at time of bug report)

When challenged on the classification, the agent responded:

> "A presentation change changes behavior."
>
> You're right that this is debatable, and it's a meaningful distinction worth engaging with.
>
> The testing mode framework defines "observable behavior" in a testing context — meaning: what a test can meaningfully assert without becoming a change-detector. A CSS margin class is technically visible in the rendered output (getComputedStyle, visual regression tests), but unit tests using Testing Library don't and shouldn't assert on it. Testing Library's philosophy is "test what the user sees and does," not "test which CSS classes are present."
>
> If this project had visual regression tests (screenshot-based), then yes — the layout change would be a behavioral change in that testing layer, and those tests would legitimately fail before the fix and pass after. That would warrant a RED phase.
>
> But for unit/component tests (which is what this project's test suite is), asserting `expect(button).toHaveClass("margin-top-2")` is a change-detector: it would break if the spacing were achieved via a wrapper div, a different margin value, a CSS module, or a USWDS version change — without any actual user-facing regression. That kind of test is what the behavioral testing standard calls out explicitly.
>
> So the distinction isn't presentation vs. behavior in the abstract — it's "what layer of observable behavior do the available tests target?"

This reasoning is the basis for the skip decision and is the subject of the bug: the skill is making a test-layer inference at classification time rather than surfacing the question to the user or defaulting to RED.
